To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the phosphoprotein of a dolphin morbilivirus (DMV), like those of other morbiliviruses, is encoded in overlapping open reading frame and is expressed as a protein with two distinct C-terminal domains; (2) the DMV phosphoprotein gene encodes two different phosphoproteins by RNA editing; and (3) the DMV P and V proteins are expressed in vivo.

a dolphin morbillivrus P gene transcript can be edited at two different sites, that the edited P transcript is translated into two proteins, and that the editing site variants found in the virus genome are different from those found in the virus mRNA.

a dolphin morbilli virus isolate exhibits genomic variation in the editing site of its phosphoprotein gene and that this variation is likely to be a consequence of the adaptation of the virus from its natural host to growth in cell culture.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of DMV pathogenesis and the development of diagnostic tests for DMV infections.
the molecular biology and evolution of morbillivirides and with the development of vaccines against these viruses.
the first report of genomic variations in morbillivirus P gene editing sites.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DMV is a virus that is capable of expressing a V protein, and that the expression of this protein can be modulated by editing the viral genome.
DMV, like other morbillivuses, has a variable editing site in the P gene and that the editing site is not a fixed feature of the DMV genome.
the DMV P mRNA is edited to encode P and V protein and the genomic RNA is edited to encode the P protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the P gene editing site of DMV is more variable than those of other morbiliviruses and that the GAGC editing site variant is not a viable DMV genome type.
the DMV P mRNA is edited at two sites in the C gene and that the editing site variants are generated by a process that is different from editing at the V gene site.
DMV, like other morbillivuses, has the capacity to produce two different proteins from the P gene by means of editing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
morbillivirses can have multiple editing site variants in a single infected cell.
the editing site of DMV is not fixed and that more than one genome type may coexist in infected cells.
the P gene of the dolphin morbillivirus is not stable and can undergo mutations that affect the editing site.
